title: Printed by the Week
passage:
Denzil Inglebeck took out teeth in hired rooms, and had his week printed on a card he left with the inns. The card gives four days: “Mondays at Haddenthorpe, Tuesdays at Nerresby, Wednesdays at Thrapmere, Thursdays at Upper and Lower Shenwold.” Nerresby stands nine miles from Haddenthorpe. Thrapmere stands thirty miles from Nerresby, and the road to it runs back through Haddenthorpe and twenty-one miles beyond. The two Shenwolds lie four miles from Haddenthorpe, ten minutes’ walk from each other. The circuit has been put down to the coach road, turnpiked in 1769, which served the three towns; its coaches changed horses at two of them. The Shenwolds sit three miles off that road, up a lane the coaches did not use. Thrapmere fills on a Wednesday and Lower Shenwold on a Thursday, and the Thursday market is the largest of the four. Upper Shenwold has no market of its own. Haddenthorpe has kept its Monday market since a charter of 1227, and Nerresby has held a Tuesday one for as long. He gave up the circuit in 1903 and took two rooms over a chemist’s shop in Haddenthorpe, where his last card gives an address and no days.
– Yasmin Oakes

questions.prompt: What does the essay imply about the circuit Inglebeck’s card sets out?

options.text: The towns’ market days fixed the order of the week, and the card follows it.
The coach road settled which market places went on the card and which stayed off it.
The Thursday is shared between two places because each of them holds its market that day.
The Tuesday market at Nerresby drew the biggest crowd of any on the card.

questions.rationale:
A is put together from two places in the essay that are never brought together. The first is the card, printed as “Mondays at Haddenthorpe, Tuesdays at Nerresby, Wednesdays at Thrapmere, Thursdays at Upper and Lower Shenwold.” The second is what the four towns do without Inglebeck, and it arrives out of order: “Thrapmere fills on a Wednesday and Lower Shenwold on a Thursday”, and then, two sentences later, “Haddenthorpe has kept its Monday market since a charter of 1227, and Nerresby has held a Tuesday one for as long.” Sort those four and each town holds one day of the week and no second one; four towns with a day each can be worked in a single sequence, and that sequence is what the card prints. The mileage stops being a puzzle at that point. A drive that goes “back through Haddenthorpe and twenty-one miles beyond” is what a Wednesday in Thrapmere costs, and a whole day divided between two places “ten minutes’ walk from each other” is what a Thursday in Shenwold costs. A puts the days first and leaves the roads to take what is left of the week.

B is the strong wrong answer, because the essay makes the coach-road case before it brings anything against it: the road was turnpiked in 1769, it “served the three towns”, and “its coaches changed horses at two of them”. The Thursday undoes it. Of the two villages the essay says that they “sit three miles off that road, up a lane the coaches did not use”, and they keep their place on the card all the same, so the road cannot be what decided who went on it. C reads the Thursday as two markets where there is one, and a single sentence refuses that: “Upper Shenwold has no market of its own.” The day belongs to Lower Shenwold, and the half of it spent in the upper village is a half spent away from a market. D is built out of the map rather than out of the text. Nerresby is nine miles from Haddenthorpe against Thrapmere at twenty-one, and the miles hand it the crowd; but the essay weighs the markets once, and the weighing falls elsewhere: “the Thursday market is the largest of the four”. A market of that size is where the people are, and on this card it falls on a Thursday.

planted_traps.A: KEY. The inference joins the card – “Mondays at Haddenthorpe, Tuesdays at Nerresby, Wednesdays at Thrapmere, Thursdays at Upper and Lower Shenwold.” – to the towns’ own weeks, which the essay supplies out of card order and in two separate sentences: “Thrapmere fills on a Wednesday and Lower Shenwold on a Thursday” and “Haddenthorpe has kept its Monday market since a charter of 1227, and Nerresby has held a Tuesday one for as long.” Four towns with one day each admit one sequence, and it is the sequence the card prints. Nothing in the passage says so; the reader has to sort the days and lay them on the card. The demoted coach road is what makes the join the only reading left, and the mileage is then a consequence rather than a blunder.
planted_traps.B: Received-account trap, and the intended strong wrong answer. The essay argues the coach-road case before it argues against it, and a reader who stops at the argument-for takes it. Refuted by: “The Shenwolds sit three miles off that road, up a lane the coaches did not use.” The Thursday stop is on the card and off the road, so the road cannot have settled what went on the card. Plausible-but-unsupported in the world: nothing outside the passage lets a reader rule it out.
planted_traps.C: Two-markets reading of one market day – the ordinary way to explain a doubled stop, and the one a reader assembles from ‘Upper and Lower’ without checking. Refuted by one sentence: “Upper Shenwold has no market of its own.” The Thursday belongs to Lower Shenwold, and the half of the day spent in the upper village is a half spent away from a market.
planted_traps.D: Map-over-text trap: Nerresby is nine miles from Haddenthorpe against Thrapmere at twenty-one, so a reader who has been counting miles gives it the crowd. Refuted by the essay’s one ranking of the markets, which points the other way: “the Thursday market is the largest of the four.” Also unrulable-out from the world, since the towns are invented.

generator_meta.opening_note: No received-explanation opening. generator_meta.motif_avoidance_note: The record’s-silence motif is NOT used, and this needed care because the unit’s subject is a calendar the card never prints. The passage nowhere says that the card omits anything, that nobody wrote it down or that the books do not say; it prints the card, prints the towns’ weeks, and leaves the reader to put them together. The argument is positive throughout. Also absent: money arithmetic of any kind (no price, no sum, no takings), the labour-drain motif, the researcher-with-survey-weakness frame, and the archive-corpus reading. No count of records, entries or people appears anywhere in the passage; its numerals are four distances, two dates and one year.
